Adult Pacific yellowtail emperor, Lethrinus atkinsoni, are reported to achieve a maximum body length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] in the waters around the western Pacific, a size that positions them among the larger members of the genus. Females become reproductively active once they reach a total length of approximately 28 cm [Lp = approximately 28 cm], a size threshold that typically corresponds with the onset of gonadal recrudescence. At this length, body mass has been estimated using length-weight relationships derived from field-sampled individuals, yielding a wet weight at puberty of 348 grams [Wwp = 348 grams]. The species is known to form spawning aggregations over reef flats during the warmer months, and spawning events are typically synchronized with the lunar cycle. Comparative studies with the closely related Lethrinus mahsena, conducted under controlled laboratory conditions, provide the best available proxy for the reproductive rate of L. atkinsoni when measured at a stable water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. Under these conditions, females release the equivalent of 227,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 227,000 eggs per spawning event] with an annual spawning frequency of one batch per year [F_R_i = one batch per year], as determined from detailed histological examination of ovarian tissue.

Neonatal life begins with the emergence of a prolarva from a pelagic, yolk-laden egg following a brief incubation period. Based on the known egg diameter of 0.7 millimeters documented in the congener Lethrinus lentjan, the wet weight at birth for Lethrinus atkinsoni is estimated to be 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This minute mass reflects the limited endogenous reserves available to the endotrophic larva before the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larva, or alevin, relies entirely on these maternally derived nutrients during the first few days post-hatching, a period characterized by rapid organogenesis and the development of the digestive tract. The transition to exotrophic feeding, marked by mouth opening and first prey capture, typically occurs once the yolk reserves are nearly exhausted, a critical point that determines early survival. Larval rearing experiments conducted at similar temperatures for other lethrinids suggest that the window for first feeding is narrow, and the timing of the trophic switch is heavily influenced by water temperature. The small initial body size of the newly hatched larva also makes it highly vulnerable to predation and starvation during the pelagic larval phase.

As individuals grow and approach the pubertal length, their body mass increases substantially. Data derived from standard length-weight regressions for the species indicate that the ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic mass attained by large adults, is approximately 1981 grams [Wwi = approximately 1981 grams]. The neonatal mass of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams] represents an exceptionally small starting point, from which individuals must increase by more than ten million-fold to reach adult size, underscoring the prodigious growth potential of this species. The relationship between length and mass follows a cubic pattern, as is typical for teleosts with isometric scaling. Large adult individuals, those approaching the maximum length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], are often caught in deeper waters adjacent to coral reef slopes, where they forage on a diet dominated by benthic invertebrates and small fishes. The attainment of this ultimate size requires several years of sustained feeding and is likely influenced by local habitat productivity and intraspecific competition for food resources. Males and females do not exhibit marked sexual dimorphism in body size, although gravid females may show a slight increase in body depth during the spawning season.

The maximum documented lifespan of the Pacific yellowtail emperor, extrapolated from otolith-based age readings and mark-recapture studies, reaches 9125 days [am = 9125 days] under ambient thermal conditions typical of its subtropical range, specifically at a mean annual water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to approximately 25 years, is considerable for a reef fish of this body size and suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward delayed senescence and repeated reproductive effort across many seasons. Aging studies indicate that growth slows markedly after the onset of sexual maturity, with most somatic energy thereafter directed toward gamete production and spawning migrations. The stable thermal environment of the Indo-West Pacific, where sea temperatures rarely deviate far from 28.6 °C, likely contributes to the relatively low metabolic costs and reduced oxidative damage that underpin this extended lifespan. In comparison, congeneric species from cooler upwelling zones tend to exhibit shorter maximum ages, implying a negative relationship between ambient temperature and longevity within the genus. Annual mortality rates for fully recruited adults are low, consistent with the species' position as a moderately K-selected teleost.

Reproductive output in this species, as inferred from studies on the closely related Lethrinus mahsena at the same thermal regime of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C], has been characterized through both fecundity estimates and spawning frequencies. Individual females are capable of producing a substantial number of eggs per spawning event, with histological analyses revealing 227,000 eggs released in a single batch [N_R_i = 227,000 eggs released in a single batch]. The frequency of these spawning events has been recorded as roughly 1 batch per year [F_R_i = roughly 1 batch per year], indicating that the species is a total or batch spawner with a clearly defined annual reproductive cycle. This relatively low spawning frequency is balanced by the high fecundity per event, a strategy that maximizes the number of offspring released during the brief period of optimal larval survival conditions. The size threshold of 28 cm [Lp = 28 cm] not only governs the onset of maturity but also influences the timing of reproductive migrations and the allocation of energy towards gametogenesis. Given the 25-year lifespan (9125 days) [am = 9125 days], a female may experience upwards of twenty spawning seasons over her lifetime, contributing significantly to population recruitment across decades at a temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C].
